summary.text: Finite Fourier inversion expresses \(nW-2a(n)\), where \(W\) counts the nonzero quadratic residues among the indexed terms, as a cotangent-weighted quadratic Gauss sum; grouping by gcd reduces it to nonnegative quadratic-character pieces, since the relevant cotangent sum is either zero or a positive multiple of \(L(1,\chi)\), with Gauss-sum evaluations and the odd/2-adic decomposition supplying the remaining signs. Thus \(2a(n)\le nW\), and \(W\le n-1\) because the term at zero vanishes, giving the stated bound after elementary integer arithmetic.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 r_n(k)=k^2\bmod n\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\},\qquad
 A(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}r_n(k).
\]
The sum in the OEIS definition is over \(1\leq k\leq n\). It is the same sum: the term at \(k=0\) is zero, the term at \(k=n\) is zero, and the other terms agree. We prove that, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
 A(n)\leq \frac{n^2-1}{2},
\]
where the quotient on the right is integer division.

The proof has two parts. The elementary last part will follow once we establish the inequality
\[
 2A(n)\leq nW(n),                                      \tag{1}
\]
where
\[
 W(n)=\#\{0\leq k<n:r_n(k)\ne0\}.
\]
The substantial part of the proof is (1). We obtain it from a Fourier formula and positivity of cotangent-weighted quadratic Gauss sums.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Quadratic Gauss sums and a Fourier identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(N\geq1\), put
\[
 \zeta_N=e^{2\pi i/N},\qquad
 G_N(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\zeta_N^{t k^2}\quad(t\in\mathbb Z).
\]
We use the convention that integer powers are allowed; of course \(\zeta_N^N=1\), so the power only depends on the exponent modulo \(N\).

We first derive the exact identity
\[
 nW(n)-2A(n)
 =\sum_{t=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{Im}G_n(t)
       \cot\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right).             \tag{2}
\]

The basic root-of-unity orthogonality relation is
\[
 \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\zeta_n^{tj}
 =\begin{cases}n,&n\mid j,\\0,&n\nmid j.\end{cases}   \tag{3}
\]
Indeed this is either a sum of \(n\) ones or a geometric progression whose ratio is a nontrivial \(n\)-th root of unity.

For \(0\leq a<n\), (3) shows that
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\zeta_n^{t(k^2-a)}
 =\begin{cases}1,&a=r_n(k),\\0,&a\ne r_n(k).\end{cases}
\]
Multiplying by \(a\), summing first over \(a\) and then over \(k\), and interchanging the finite sums gives
\[
 A(n)=\frac1n\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}G_n(t)
       \sum_{a=0}^{n-1}a\zeta_n^{-ta}.                 \tag{4}
\]
The term \(t=0\) is
\[
 \frac1nG_n(0)\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}a=\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
If \(1\leq t<n\), set \(z=\zeta_n^{-t}\). Then \(z^n=1\) and \(z\ne1\). Differentiating the finite geometric sum, or directly shifting indices, gives
\[
 (z-1)\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}az^a=n.
\]
Consequently (4) becomes
\[
 A(n)=\frac{n(n-1)}2+
       \sum_{t=1}^{n-1}\frac{G_n(t)}{\zeta_n^{-t}-1}.  \tag{5}
\]

We also count the zero quadratic residues occurring in the list. By (3),
\[
 \#\{0\leq k<n:n\mid k^2\}
 =1+\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n-1}G_n(t).                    \tag{6}
\]
Since \(W(n)\) is \(n\) minus this number, substituting (5) and (6), and using
\[
 \frac{\zeta_n^{-t}+1}{\zeta_n^{-t}-1}
   =i\cot\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right),             \tag{7}
\]
we obtain
\[
 nW(n)-2A(n)
 =-\sum_{t=1}^{n-1}G_n(t)i\cot\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right).
\]
The left side is real. Taking real parts on the right, and noting that the cotangent is real, gives (2), because
\(\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z\).
Identity (7) follows immediately by putting \(e^{-2i\theta}=\zeta_n^{-t}\) with \(\theta=\pi t/n\), or from the exponential formula for cotangent.

Thus (1) will follow if the right side of (2) is nonnegative.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Reduction to sums over integers coprime to a modulus
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For every positive integer \(m\), define
\[
 P(m)=\sum_{\substack{1\leq s<m\\(s,m)=1}}
       \operatorname{Im}G_m(s)\cot\!\left(\frac{\pi s}{m}\right). \tag{8}
\]
We claim that
\[
 P(m)\geq0\qquad\text{for every }m\geq1.              \tag{9}
\]
Before proving this, let us see why it implies the required nonnegativity in (2).

Partition \(1\leq t<n\) according to
\[
 m=\frac{n}{(t,n)}.
\]
For a fixed divisor \(m\mid n\), put \(d=n/m\). The integers in this fiber are exactly \(t=ds\), where \(1\leq s<m\) and \((s,m)=1\). Moreover,
\[
 \cot\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{n}\right)
 =\cot\!\left(\frac{\pi s}{m}\right),                \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
 G_n(ds)=dG_m(s).                                      \tag{11}
\]
To prove (11), write every \(k\in\{0,\dots,dm-1\}\) uniquely according to its residue modulo \(m\). The summand
\(e^{2\pi i ds k^2/(dm)}=e^{2\pi i s k^2/m}\)
depends only on that residue, and each residue occurs exactly \(d\) times. Hence the contribution of the fiber is
\[
 dP(m)=\frac nmP(m).
\]
Summing over all divisors \(m\mid n\), (2) becomes
\[
 nW(n)-2A(n)=\sum_{m\mid n}\frac nmP(m).               \tag{12}
\]
Thus (9) indeed proves (1).

It remains to prove (9).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. A positivity lemma for quadratic characters
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A quadratic Dirichlet character modulo \(m\) will mean a multiplicative function \(\chi\) on residue classes modulo \(m\), zero on nonunits and taking values \(\pm1\) on units, such that \(\chi^2=1\) on the unit group.

We need the following lemma.

Lemma. Suppose \(m\geq2\), \(\chi\) is a quadratic Dirichlet character modulo \(m\),
\[
 \operatorname{Im}G_m(s)=\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)\chi(s)
 \quad\text{whenever }(s,m)=1,                         \tag{13}
\]
and \(\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)\geq0\). Then \(P(m)\geq0\).

Proof. Since \(\chi\) vanishes on nonunits,
\[
 C(\chi):=\sum_{j\bmod m}\chi(j)
          \cot\!\left(\frac{\pi j}{m}\right)
 =\sum_{\substack{1\leq j<m\\(j,m)=1}}\chi(j)
          \cot\!\left(\frac{\pi j}{m}\right).         \tag{14}
\]
(The apparent \(j=0\) term is understood as zero because \(\chi(0)=0\); equivalently one simply uses the right side.) By (13),
\[
 P(m)=\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)\,C(\chi).               \tag{15}
\]
We show \(C(\chi)\geq0\).

If \(\chi(-1)=1\), pairing \(j\) with \(-j\), and using
\(\cot(\pi- x)=-\cot x\), gives \(C(\chi)=0\).

If \(\chi(-1)=-1\), the standard finite cotangent formula for a Dirichlet \(L\)-value is
\[
 C(\chi)=\frac{2m}{\pi}L(1,\chi).                      \tag{16}
\]
For completeness, this formula follows from
\[
 \pi\cot(\pi a)=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}\frac1{a+r}
\]
interpreted by symmetric pairing. For \(0<a<1\), the paired, absolutely convergent form is
\[
 \frac{\pi}{2}\cot(\pi a)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac12
   \left(\frac1{r+a}-\frac1{r+1-a}\right).            \tag{17}
\]
Insert \(a=j/m\), multiply by the odd character \(\chi(j)\), and sum over residues. Regrouping the resulting terms according to integers congruent to \(j\) and \(-j\) modulo \(m\) yields (16).

Finally, \(L(1,\chi)>0\) for a nontrivial real quadratic character. Here is the positivity argument used in this proof. For real \(x>1\),
\[
 \zeta(x)L(x,\chi)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{b(r)}{r^x},
 \qquad b(r)=\sum_{d\mid r}\chi(d).
\]
Every \(b(r)\) is nonnegative. This can be checked prime-power by prime-power: if \(\chi(p)=1\), the local divisor sum is \(e+1\); if \(\chi(p)=0\), it is \(1\); and if \(\chi(p)=-1\), it is \(1\) for even \(e\) and \(0\) for odd \(e\). Also \(b(1)=1\), so the displayed Dirichlet series is positive. Since \(\zeta(x)>0\), this gives \(L(x,\chi)>0\) for \(x>1\). The Dirichlet \(L\)-function of a nontrivial character is continuous at \(1\), hence \(L(1,\chi)\geq0\); its standard nonvanishing at \(1\) makes the inequality strict. Thus (16) is positive. Therefore in both parity cases \(C(\chi)\geq0\), and (15), together with \(\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)\geq0\), proves the lemma. \(\square\)

We now verify the hypotheses of this lemma for every modulus. This requires the relevant quadratic Gauss-sum formulas.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Gauss-sum formulas
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We use three standard facts, and include their derivations or reductions.

First, for every \(N\geq1\),
\[
 G_N(1)=\frac{\sqrt N(1+i)}2\bigl(1+(-i)^N\bigr).      \tag{18}
\]
In particular,
\[
 \operatorname{Im}G_N(1)\geq0.                        \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, according as \(N\equiv0,1,2,3\pmod4\), the factor
\(1+(-i)^N\) is respectively \(2,1-i,0,1+i\). Thus the imaginary part in (18) is respectively \(\sqrt N,0,0,\sqrt N\).

For reference, (18) may be derived without assuming that \(N\) is odd as follows. For \(\varepsilon>0\), consider the regularized theta series
\[
 \Theta_N(\varepsilon)=
 \sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}
 \exp\!\left[-\pi\left(\varepsilon-\frac{2i}{N}\right)r^2\right].
\]
Grouping \(r\) by its residue \(k\pmod N\) gives
\[
 \Theta_N(\varepsilon)=
 \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i k^2/N}
 \sum_{q\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi\varepsilon(k+Nq)^2}.
\]
The elementary shifted-theta limit
\[
 \sqrt u\sum_{q\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi u(q+x)^2}\longrightarrow1
 \quad(u\downarrow0)
\]
therefore yields
\[
 \sqrt\varepsilon\,\Theta_N(\varepsilon)
 \longrightarrow \frac{G_N(1)}N.                     \tag{20}
\]
On the other hand, Poisson summation for a Gaussian says, when \(\Re b>0\),
\[
 \sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi b r^2}
 =b^{-1/2}\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi r^2/b},         \tag{21}
\]
with the principal square root. Apply this with
\(b=\varepsilon-2i/N\), split the dual sum into even and odd integers, and again use the shifted-theta limit. The two surviving phases are \(1\) and
\(e^{-\pi iN/2}=(-i)^N\). One obtains
\[
 \frac{G_N(1)}N=(-2iN)^{-1/2}\bigl(1+(-i)^N\bigr).
\]
Since the principal value satisfies
\((-2iN)^{-1/2}=(1+i)/(2\sqrt N)\), this is exactly (18). All uses of limits above are justified by Gaussian domination; after residue-class splitting the relevant tails are bounded by convergent Gaussian series.

Second, if \(u\) is odd, \((u,M)=1\), and \(M\) is odd, then
\[
 G_M(u)=\left(\frac{u}{M}\right)G_M(1),               \tag{22}
\]
where \((u/M)\) is the Jacobi symbol. One way to prove this is first to handle an odd prime \(p\). Grouping \(x\) according to \(x^2\) shows that multiplication of the quadratic phase by \(u\) multiplies the Gauss sum by the Legendre symbol \((u/p)\). For \(p^e\), splitting \(x=a+p^{e-1}c\) and summing the resulting geometric progression gives the recurrence
\[
 G_{p^e}(u)=pG_{p^{e-2}}(u)\quad(e\ge2),               \tag{23}
\]
and the same recurrence for \(u=1\). This yields the factor \((u/p)^e\), which is \((u/p^e)\). Finally, for coprime moduli \(M_1,M_2\), the Chinese remainder theorem factors a Gauss sum into the two component Gauss sums, with harmless unit multipliers determined by Bézout coefficients. Multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol cancels the same multipliers in the ratio. This proves (22) for every odd \(M\).

Third, for odd \(u\) and \(j\ge1\), direct evaluation at moduli \(4\) and \(8\), followed by the recurrence
\[
 G_{2^a}(u)=2G_{2^{a-2}}(u)\quad(a\ge4),               \tag{24}
\]
gives
\[
 G_{2^{2j}}(u)=2^j(1+i^u),                             \tag{25}
\]
\[
 G_{2^{2j+1}}(u)=2^{j+1}\zeta_8^u,                    \tag{26}
\]
where \(\zeta_8=e^{\pi i/4}\). To see (24), split the summation variable into classes differing by \(2^{a-2}\). The inner four-term geometric sum vanishes for odd intermediate classes and equals four for even ones; after replacing an even variable by twice a new variable, the result reduces to twice the Gauss sum modulo \(2^{a-2}\). The base cases are
\[
 G_4(u)=2(1+i^u),\qquad G_8(u)=4\zeta_8^u,
\]
which follow by listing the four or eight squares. Thus (25) and (26) follow by induction.

We shall express the signs in (25) and (26) by the real quadratic characters
\[
 \chi_4(u)=\begin{cases}1,&u\equiv1\pmod4,\\-1,&u\equiv3\pmod4,\end{cases}
\]
\[
 \chi_8(u)=\begin{cases}1,&u\equiv1,7\pmod8,\\-1,&u\equiv3,5\pmod8,\end{cases}
\]
and
\[
 \chi'_8(u)=\begin{cases}1,&u\equiv1,3\pmod8,\\-1,&u\equiv5,7\pmod8.\end{cases}
\]
For odd \(u\), elementary trigonometry gives
\[
 \operatorname{Im}(i^u)=\chi_4(u),                    \tag{27}
\]
\[
 \operatorname{Re}(\zeta_8^u)=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\chi_8(u),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Im}(\zeta_8^u)=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\chi'_8(u). \tag{28}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Proof that \(P(m)\geq0\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The cases \(m=0,1\) contain no terms in (8); for our application only positive \(m\) occurs, and \(P(1)=0\). Assume now \(m\ge2\).

Case 1: \(m\) is odd.

Take \(\chi(s)=(s/m)\), the Jacobi character. It is quadratic. Formula (22) gives
\[
 \operatorname{Im}G_m(s)=\left(\frac{s}{m}\right)
                          \operatorname{Im}G_m(1)
\]
for every \((s,m)=1\). Together with (19), the character-positivity lemma proves \(P(m)\geq0\).

Case 2: \(m\equiv2\pmod4\).

Write \(m=2m_0\) with \(m_0\) odd. If \((s,m)=1\), then \(s\) is odd. The Chinese remainder factorization of the Gauss sum contains the factor
\[
 G_2(u)=1+(-1)^u=0
\]
for an odd unit \(u\). Hence \(G_m(s)=0\) for every unit \(s\), including \(s=1\). Thus every term of \(P(m)\) is zero and \(P(m)=0\). (Equivalently, one may apply the positivity lemma with any quadratic character.)

Case 3: \(4\mid m\).

Write uniquely
\[
 m=2^a m_0,
 \qquad a\ge2,
 \qquad m_0\text{ odd}.                               \tag{29}
\]
Choose integers \(\alpha,\beta\) with
\[
 \alpha m_0+\beta2^a=1.                               \tag{30}
\]
Then \(\alpha\) is odd and \(\beta\) is coprime to \(m_0\). The Chinese remainder theorem gives, for every integer \(s\),
\[
 G_m(s)=G_{2^a}(\alpha s)G_{m_0}(\beta s).             \tag{31}
\]
For \((s,m)=1\), use (22) in the odd factor:
\[
 G_m(s)=G_{2^a}(\alpha s)
 \left(\frac{\beta s}{m_0}\right)G_{m_0}(1).         \tag{32}
\]
The fixed sign \((\beta/m_0)\) and the fixed character values at \(\alpha\) will occur both at \(s\) and at \(1\), so they cancel when we compare imaginary parts. We now perform the four necessary subcases.

From (18), because \(m_0\) is odd,
\[
 G_{m_0}(1)=
 \begin{cases}
 \sqrt{m_0},&m_0\equiv1\pmod4,\\
 i\sqrt{m_0},&m_0\equiv3\pmod4.
 \end{cases}                                           \tag{33}
\]

(a) \(a=2j\) is even and \(m_0\equiv1\pmod4\). By (25), (27), and (33),
\[
 \operatorname{Im}\bigl(G_{2^a}(\alpha s)G_{m_0}(1)\bigr)
 =2^j\sqrt{m_0}\,\chi_4(\alpha s).
\]
By multiplicativity, \(\chi_4(\alpha s)=\chi_4(\alpha)\chi_4(s)\). Inserting this into (32) shows
\[
 \operatorname{Im}G_m(s)=\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)
 \left(\frac{s}{m_0}\right)\chi_4(s).                \tag{34}
\]
Thus (13) holds for the quadratic character obtained by lifting the Jacobi character modulo \(m_0\) and multiplying it by the lifted \(\chi_4\).

(b) \(a=2j\) is even and \(m_0\equiv3\pmod4\). Now multiplying \(1+i^{\alpha s}\) by \(i\sqrt{m_0}\), and using that the real part of \(i^{\alpha s}\) is zero for odd \(\alpha s\), gives
\[
 \operatorname{Im}\bigl(G_{2^a}(\alpha s)G_{m_0}(1)\bigr)
 =2^j\sqrt{m_0},
\]
independent of \(s\). Hence
\[
 \operatorname{Im}G_m(s)=\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)
 \left(\frac{s}{m_0}\right).                         \tag{35}
\]
Here the required quadratic character is just the Jacobi character modulo \(m_0\), lifted to modulus \(m\).

(c) \(a=2j+1\) is odd and \(m_0\equiv1\pmod4\). Since \(a\ge3\), formula (26), followed by (28) and (33), gives
\[
 \operatorname{Im}\bigl(G_{2^a}(\alpha s)G_{m_0}(1)\bigr)
 =2^{j+1}\sqrt{m_0}\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\chi'_8(\alpha s).
\]
Using multiplicativity of \(\chi'_8\), (32) yields
\[
 \operatorname{Im}G_m(s)=\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)
 \left(\frac{s}{m_0}\right)\chi'_8(s).               \tag{36}
\]
Thus we use the product of the lifted Jacobi character and the lifted \(\chi'_8\).

(d) \(a=2j+1\) is odd and \(m_0\equiv3\pmod4\). Multiplication by the \(i\) in (33) changes the imaginary part into the real part of \(\zeta_8^{\alpha s}\). Therefore (28) gives
\[
 \operatorname{Im}G_m(s)=\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)
 \left(\frac{s}{m_0}\right)\chi_8(s).                \tag{37}
\]
The required character is the product of the lifted Jacobi character and lifted \(\chi_8\).

Each character in (34)--(37) is quadratic: it is a product of characters taking values \(\pm1\) on units, and lifting a character from a divisor of \(m\) preserves this property. Thus in every subcase relation (13) holds. Formula (19) supplies \(\operatorname{Im}G_m(1)\geq0\), so the character-positivity lemma gives \(P(m)\geq0\).

The odd, \(2\bmod4\), and \(0\bmod4\) cases exhaust all positive integers. This proves (9).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Completion of the arithmetic argument
--------------------------------------------------------------------

By (12) and (9),
\[
 nW(n)-2A(n)\geq0,
\]
so
\[
 2A(n)\leq nW(n).                                     \tag{38}
\]
There is also a direct residue interpretation of this inequality. Define the negative-residue sum
\[
 B(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}((-k^2)\bmod n)
     =\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(n-r_n(k))\bmod n.
\]
For each \(k\), if \(r_n(k)=0\), then both \(r_n(k)\) and its negative residue are zero; if \(r_n(k)\ne0\), their sum is \(n\). Therefore
\[
 A(n)+B(n)=nW(n).                                     \tag{39}
\]
Combining (38) and (39) also says \(A(n)\leq B(n)\), which is the comparison underlying the proof.

Finally, \(k=0\) never contributes to \(W(n)\), because \(r_n(0)=0\). Since there are only \(n-1\) remaining values of \(k\),
\[
 W(n)\leq n-1.                                       \tag{40}
\]
It follows from (38) and (40) that
\[
 2A(n)\leq n(n-1).                                   \tag{41}
\]
For \(n\geq1\),
\[
 n(n-1)=n^2-n\leq n^2-1.                             \tag{42}
\]
Thus
\[
 2A(n)\leq n^2-1.
\]
Because \(A(n)\) is an integer, this is equivalent to
\[
 A(n)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n^2-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
The numerator \(n^2-1\) is in fact always even when \(n\) is odd; when \(n\) is even the displayed floor is exactly the stipulated integer division. This is the desired inequality. As observed at the start, \(A(n)\) is the same as \(\sum_{k=1}^n(k^2\bmod n)\), so the result applies to the OEIS sequence exactly as stated.
